title_en: Shanghai Animation Film Studio v. Zhuhai Skywalker Culture Communication Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over infringement of copyright property rights
ruling_gist_en: Animation film character images may be protected as artistic works under the Copyright Law; and only citizens who have made original contributions to such character images may qualify as authors. In the planned economy era prior to the enactment and implementation of the Copyright Law, there was neither the conceptual foundation nor the institutional environment to protect authors' rights. Therefore, when a people's court determines the ownership of copyright in the property rights of character images in animation films created during this specific historical period, it shall, in the application of law, employ the method of interest balancing, comprehensively considering various factors such as history, current status, and fairness, so as to achieve a balance between individual rights and collective interests.

full_text_en:
Shanghai Art Film Studio v. Zhuhai Tianxingzhe Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. et al.

— Dispute over infringement of copyright property rights

Ruling Summary

The character images in animated films can be protected as works of fine art under the Copyright Law; and only the citizens who have made unique creative contributions to such character images can be the authors. During the era of the planned economy preceding the enactment and implementation of the Copyright Law, there was neither the conceptual foundation nor the institutional environment for protecting the rights of authors. Therefore, when determining the ownership of copyright property rights in animated film character images created during this specific historical period, a People's Court must apply the method of balancing interests in the process of legal application, comprehensively considering various factors including history, the current situation, and fairness, to achieve a balance between individual rights and collective interests.

Plaintiff: Shanghai Art Film Studio; domicile: Wanhangdu Road, Jing'an District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Wang Tianyun, responsible person of the studio.

Defendant: Zhuhai Tianxingzhe Cultural Communication Co., Ltd.; domicile: Jida Shuwan Road, Zhuhai City.
Legal Representative: Tang Zebo, Chairman of the Board.

Defendant: Zhuhai Wukong Apparel Co., Ltd.; domicile: Zhuhai Xiangzhou Zijing Road.
Legal Representative: Wu Hongming.

Defendant: Zhuhai Qianzhi Footwear Co., Ltd.; domicile: Shuanglin Section, Liangang Industrial Zone, Jinwan District, Zhuhai City.
Legal Representative: Huang Jinshui.

Defendant: Shanghai Yangpai Trading Co., Ltd.; domicile: Humin Road, Minhang District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Sun Lintao, Executive Director of the Company.

Defendant: Shanghai Jiulv Trade Development Co., Ltd.; domicile: Jiangchuan Road, Minhang District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Chen Jinghao, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Plaintiff Shanghai Art Film Studio (hereinafter referred to as the Art Film Studio) filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court against Defendants Zhuhai Tianxingzhe Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianxingzhe Company), Zhuhai Wukong Apparel Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Wukong Company), Zhuhai Qianzhi Footwear Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Qianzhi Company), Shanghai Yangpai Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yangpai Company), and Shanghai Jiulv Trade Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jiulv Company) regarding a dispute over infringement of copyright property rights.

Plaintiff Art Film Studio alleged: The Plaintiff is the producer of the animated film "Havoc in Heaven" and lawfully holds the copyright in the fine art work of the Sun Wukong character image from "Havoc in Heaven." In June 2001, the Plaintiff authorized Defendant Tianxingzhe Company the exclusive distribution rights for the "Havoc in Heaven" film in the United States. In 2008, the Plaintiff discovered that Tianxingzhe Company had, without authorization, used the Sun Wukong character image and numerous deformed images adapted from it on its website with the domain name www.wukongland.com. Defendant Wukong Company was established with investment from Tianxingzhe Company; it operated a website with the domain name www.wukongkids.com and established sales agents nationwide, using the website and various local agency outlets to promote infringing products manufactured by Qianzhi Company, on a large sales scale. Defendants Tianxingzhe Company, Wukong Company, and Qianzhi Company also promoted and disseminated the infringing acts against the Plaintiff's copyright through media and their respective websites at various large-scale events such as exhibitions, trade fairs, and promotional conferences. Defendants Yangpai Company and Jiulv Company jointly engaged in the sale of the infringing products, constituting joint infringement. The Plaintiff hereby petitions the court for judgment: 1. Order all Defendants to immediately cease their infringing acts; 2. Order all Defendants to jointly compensate the Plaintiff for economic losses and reasonable expenses totaling over RMB 5,156,000; 3. Order all Defendants to publish an apology statement to the Plaintiff publicly in the Xinmin Evening News.

Defendant Tianxingzhe Company argued: The fine art work of the Sun Wukong character image was created by Zhang Guangyu, with copyright belonging to Zhang Guangyu; therefore, the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, lacks standing to sue. The "Wukong" cartoon character image designed by the Defendant is different from the "Sun Wukong" character image in "Havoc in Heaven" for which the Plaintiff claims rights. The Defendant lawfully holds patent rights, trademark rights, and copyright in the "Wukong" cartoon character image and has not infringed the Plaintiff's copyright. The Defendant requests the court to dismiss the Plaintiff's claims.

Defendants Wukong Company and Qianzhi Company did not appear in court and did not submit written defense statements.

Defendants Yangpai Company and Jiulv Company jointly argued: The copyright in the fine art work of the Sun Wukong character image belongs to Zhang Guangyu; therefore, the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, lacks standing to sue. Yangpai Company leased its store space in the shopping mall to Jiulv Company for business operations. The children's shoes products sold by Jiulv Company, which were manufactured by Wukong Company, had a legitimate source. The two Defendants did not share a common intent with the other three Defendants, nor were they negligent. They should not bear compensation liability according to law.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts in the first instance:

In 1945, Zhang Guangyu (1900-1965, one of the founders of modern Chinese decorative art, an outstanding cartoonist) created a color mythological comic serial titled "Journey to the West Sketchbook." This work consisted of sixty cartoons, each with textual explanations. It adopted the form of the classic "Journey to the West," borrowing its story structure and major mythological characters from the original cast of "Journey to the West." The work included character images of the four pilgrims, including Tang Sanzang and his disciples. The key features of the Sun Wukong image were: wearing a headband, a light green scarf around the neck, a yellow upper garment, a tiger-skin short skirt around the waist, bright red trousers, and black boots on the feet. The face was oval-shaped, with a heart-shaped red mark in the center of the face, curved black eyebrows above, and a circle of gold around the eyes.

Between 1960 and 1964, the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, created and completed the animated film "Havoc in Heaven" based on the classic episode from "Journey to the West." During this period, Wan Laiming, the director of the Art Film Studio, invited brothers Zhang Guangyu and Zhang Zhengyu to participate in the artistic design. The Sun Wukong character image for "Havoc in Heaven" was finalized by Yan Dingxian, an employee of the Art Film Studio, in 1961. Parts 1 and 2 of "Havoc in Heaven" were publicly released in 1961 and 1964, respectively. The key features of the Sun Wukong character image in the film were: wearing a headband, a bright green scarf around the neck, a yellow upper garment, a tiger-skin short skirt around the waist, bright red trousers, and black boots on the feet. The face was peach-shaped, with two curved contour lines for the upper half and one curved contour line for the lower half. There was a heart-shaped red mark in the center of the face, crescent-shaped green eyebrows above, and a circle of gold around the eyes. The vertical central axis of the eyes and the tip of the nose formed an inverted triangle.

The film catalog (1950-1970) compiled and printed by the Shanghai Film Bureau in 1982 recorded: Part 1 of the animated film "Havoc in Heaven": Artistic Design: Zhang Guangyu; Animation Design: Yan Dingxian, Duan Jun, Pu Jiaxiang, Lu Qing, Lin Wenxiao, Ge Guiyun; Part 2 of the animated film "Havoc in Heaven": Animation Design or Puppet Design: Yan Dingxian, Pu Jiaxiang, Lin Wenxiao, Duan Jun, Lu Qing, Zhang Shimin, Yan Shanchun. Except for Zhang Guangyu, all other credited personnel were employees of the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio.

The certification statements provided by the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, during the litigation, signed by Yan Dingxian, Pu Jiaxiang, Lin Wenxiao, and Lu Qing, stated that the artistic design for the animated film "Havoc in Heaven" was by Zhang Guangyu and Zhang Zhengyu; the animation design was by Yan Dingxian, Lin Wenxiao, Pu Jiaxiang, Lu Qing, and Ge Guiyun. All rights in this work, except the right of authorship, belong to the Art Film Studio.

The VCDs for the Sun Wukong series "Sun Wukong's Havoc in Heaven," Parts 1 and 2, and the 2004 Classic Retrospective "40th Anniversary Collection Gift Box" DVD of "Havoc in Heaven," published and distributed by Shanghai Film Audio-Video Publishing House, showed that the producer credited on the outer packaging boxes and the discs was the Art Film Studio. When played in court, the VCD film showed the artistic design credit as Zhang Guangyu; the DVD film showed the artistic design credits as Zhang Guangyu and Zhang Zhengyu.

On June 18, 2001, the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, and Guangzhou Tianxingzhe Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Guangzhou Tianxingzhe Company) signed a Film Distribution Rights Assignment Contract, stipulating that the Art Film Studio would assign the exclusive film distribution rights for the animated film "Havoc in Heaven" in the United States to Guangzhou Tianxingzhe Company. The authorization period was five years, from August 1, 2001, to July 31, 2006.

On April 14, 2008, Tang Zebo (Chairman of Tianxingzhe Company), using Zhuhai Sky Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. as the copyright owner, voluntarily registered the WuKong series of cartoon images he had designed with the Guangdong Provincial Copyright Protection Union, under registration number 19-2008-F-0428. Among these was an image of Sun Wukong pointing to the right with his right hand, holding the Golden Cudgel diagonally behind him with his left hand (hereinafter referred to as the Filed Registered Sun Wukong Image).

On January 13, 2009, Zhuhai Sky Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. applied for and registered Trademark No. 7162768, a combined graphic and text mark "WUK + Simplified Sun Wukong Head Silhouette + NG" (hereinafter referred to as the Combined Graphic and Text Mark No. 7162768). The international classification was Class 25, covering goods such as clothing, baby textile diapers, shoes, and hats.

On February 23, 2010, under the on-site supervision of a notary public, the Plaintiff's authorized representative used Baidu to search for "Wukong Apparel," accessed the website at www.wukongkids.com. The website's homepage displayed the identifier "Boldfaced Combined Graphic and Text Mark No. 7162768 + Wukong Apparel," a series of children's shoes, and a screenshot of the Sun Wukong character image from the "Havoc in Heaven" animated film. Upon entering the home page, the title bar read "Wukong Company." The page featured sections such as About Us, Corporate News, Product Showcase, Franchise Information, etc. Clicking on the "About Us - Company Background" section revealed text stating: "Qianzhi Company was founded in 2001. In 2004, it built modern factory buildings, dormitories, and two advanced sports shoe production lines, with a total building area exceeding 13,700 square meters. It mainly produces children's shoes, various types of sports and casual shoes for men and women, exporting to developed countries and regions such as Japan, Europe, and the United States, with cumulative shoe exports exceeding 10 million pairs. In the summer of 2008, it obtained the license to operate the 'Wukong Children's Shoes' brand through Tianxingzhe International Communication Agency." Searching for "Tianxingzhe International Communication Agency" on Baidu led to the website at www.wukongland.com. The website's homepage displayed the logo of the Combined Graphic and Text Mark No. 7162768 and a Sun Wukong cartoon image. The title bar read "Zhuhai Sky Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. / Zhuhai Tianxingzhe International Communication Agency / Tang Zeming / wukong / Tianxingzhe / Wukong Official Website" and other content. The page featured sections such as News Center, About Us, Brand Licensing, Product Showcase, Download Area, Share Surprises, etc. From the home page, entering the "Company History" section under "About Us" revealed sections for "Glorious Imprints" and "Milestones." The "Milestones" section recorded: In 2001, Tianxingzhe founder Mr. Tang Zemin bought out the overseas distribution rights and adaptation rights for the classic animation "Havoc in Heaven" and registered "WuKong." From March 2006 to April 2008, "Wukong" won various awards including "China Animation Industry Top Ten Influential Brands," "Asia Youth Animation Contest Best Image Finalist Award," and "2007 China Creative Industry Annual Awards Top Ten Potential Brands." The bottom right corner of the page displayed the Filed Registered Sun Wukong Image. The Shanghai Oriental Notary Public Office issued Notarial Certificate (2010) Hu Dong Zheng Jing Zi No. 1442 for the above notarization process.

On October 13, 2010, under the supervision of a notary public, the Plaintiff's authorized representative accessed the "Public Inquiry" section of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology's ICP/IP Address/Domain Name Information Filing Management System. The inquiry showed: website homepage address www.wukongland.com, with the filing entity being Tianxingzhe Company, website name being Tianxingzhe Company, review time being October 23, 2009; website homepage address www.wukongkids.com, with the filing entity being Qianzhi Company, website name being Wukong Apparel, review time being August 9, 2009. Accessing the www.wukongland.com website revealed the same homepage content as reflected in Notarial Certificate (2010) Hu Dong Zheng Jing Zi No. 1442. The Shanghai Oriental Notary Public Office issued Notarial Certificate (2010) Hu Dong Zheng Jing Zi No. 9110 for the above notarization process.

Defendant Yangpai Company operated the YOUNG PARK shopping mall located within the Bailian South Shopping Center at No. 7388 Humin Road, Shanghai, and provided Store No. A13-1 within it to Defendant Jiulv Company for business operations, for a term from June 25, 2009, to July 31, 2010.

On May 24, 2009, Defendant Wukong Company authorized Defendant Jiulv Company to sell the "Wukong Children's Shoes" it produced. The authorization period was from May 24, 2009, to May 23, 2019. The Trademark Registration Acceptance Notice provided by Jiulv Company indicated that the application for registration of the Combined Graphic and Text Mark No. 7162768 by Zhuhai Sky Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. had been accepted by the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce. This notice bore the official seal of Wukong Company. An inspection report from the Guangdong Zhuhai Quality and Metrology Supervision and Testing Institute showed that the producing unit of the Wukong Children's Shoes was Defendant Qianzhi Company.

On February 25, 2010, under the on-site supervision of a notary public, the Plaintiff's authorized representative purchased a pair of Wukong Children's Shoes sold by Defendant Jiulv Company on the fourth floor of the Bailian South Shopping Center at No. 7388 Humin Road, Shanghai, for a price of RMB 128. The Shanghai Oriental Notary Public Office issued Notarial Certificate (2010) Hu Dong Zheng Jing Zi No. 1493 for the above notarization process. Upon in-court inspection, the upper left corner of the front of the shoe box read "Wukong Image Licensed by Tianxingzhe International Communication Agency"; the middle-left part of the front bore the words "Wukong Children's Shoes" and the boldfaced Combined Graphic and Text Mark No. 7162768 logo; the right part of the front bore the Filed Registered Wukong Image. The left side of the bottom of the box indicated "Wukong Company, Address: Room 301, Kehui Building, No. 63 Zijing Road, Xiangzhou District, Zhuhai City, Website: www.wukongkids.com"; the right side bore the Wukong image shown on the front of the box, with the URL: http://www.wukongland.com below it. Upon opening the box, it contained a pair of children's shoes, with a Wukong head image attached to the tongue of the shoe; the inner bottom of the shoe bore the boldfaced Combined Graphic and Text Mark No. 7162768 logo; one shoe had a plastic Wukong image figurine and a picture card bearing the Wukong image attached to it (the said Wukong image being identical to the one on the front of the box); the front side of the three-guarantee quality tag stated "Wukong Image Licensed by Tianxingzhe International Communication Agency; Wukong Company, Address: Room 301, Kehui Building, No. 63 Zijing Road, Xiangzhou District, Zhuhai City; Tel: 0756-2512038 Fax: 0756-2512028; Website: www.wukongkids.com," and other content.

During the litigation, the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, specified that the work of fine art it sought to protect was the Sun Wukong character image and provided screenshots from the film "Havoc in Heaven" for illustration.

Following a comparison in court, the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, alleged that the Wukong character image used by the five Defendants shared the same key features as the Sun Wukong character image the Art Film Studio sought to protect, constituting material similarity.

The main issues in dispute in the first instance of this case were: 1. Whether the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, had standing in this case; 2. Whether the acts committed by the five Defendants infringed upon the Art Film Studio's copyright; 3. If infringement was established, what civil liability should the five Defendants bear.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held in the first instance:

I. Regarding whether the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, had standing in this case

This case concerns a dispute over infringement of copyright property rights. The key to whether the Plaintiff, Art Film Studio, has standing to sue lies in whether the Art Film Studio holds the copyright in the fine art work of the Sun Wukong character image from the animated film "Havoc in Heaven." According to Article 11 of the Copyright Law, the citizen who creates a work is the author. In the absence of proof to the contrary, the citizen, legal entity, or other organization that appears as the author on the work is considered the author. In this case, what the Art Film Studio seeks to protect is the copyright in the Sun Wukong character image from the animated film "Havoc in Heaven." This character image is an animated design, falling under the category of a work of fine art. According to the relevant evidence provided by the Art Film Studio, the designer of this fine art work was Zhang Guangyu, or Zhang Guangyu and Zhang Zhengyu. Based on the statements of both parties, when producing the "Havoc in Heaven" animated film, the Art Film Studio invited Zhang Guangyu to participate in the design of the film's character images, given his expertise in creating the Sun Wukong character image. Zhang Zhengyu participated in the character image design at a later stage. Considering Zhang Guangyu's pre-existing foundation in creating the Sun Wukong character image, the protracted production period of the animated film, and the fact that the brothers Zhang Guangyu and Zhang Zhengyu participated in its creation successively, the court confirms that the creator of this fine art work is Zhang Guangyu. Concurrently, considering that the final finalized version of the Sun Wukong character image was completed by Yan Dingxian, an employee of the Art Film Studio, and that the finalized animated Sun Wukong character image is fundamentally identical to the comic Sun Wukong character image created by Zhang Guangyu in "Journey to the West Sketchbook" in terms of character portrayal, costume, and other basic elements, reflecting a continuity of creative ideas, and given that Zhang Guangyu's and Yan Dingxian's design of the Sun Wukong animated character image was both for the purpose of completing the Art Film Studio's production task for the "Havoc in Heaven" animated film, and that Yan Dingxian has explicitly stated that the copyright property rights in this work belong to the Art Film Studio, therefore, the copyright property rights in the Sun Wukong character image from the animated film "Havoc in Heaven" shall be jointly held by Zhang Guangyu and the Art Film Studio. Accordingly, the Art Film Studio has standing to sue in this case and has the right to initiate a copyright infringement lawsuit.

II. Regarding whether the five Defendants infringed the copyright

... (To be continued in Part 2)

First, Zhang Guangyu and the plaintiff, Meiying Film Studio, created the Monkey King character image for the animated film *Havoc in Heaven* between 1960 and 1961, far earlier than when Tang Zebo, the legal representative of Tiansing Company, designed the WuKong series of cartoon images. Second, the defendant Tiansing Company publicly stated on its website: "In 2001, Tiansing founder Tang Zemin bought the overseas distribution rights and adaptation rights of the classic animation *Havoc in Heaven*, and registered 'WuKong'." During the trial, Tiansing Company failed to provide a reasonable explanation for the above content appearing on its website. Third, upon comparison during the trial, the Monkey King character images appearing on the websites of Tiansing Company and the defendant Qianzhi Company, as well as the Monkey King character images on the packaging boxes and pendants of the Wukong children's shoes sold by the defendant Jiulü Company, are substantially identical in main features such as the character's physical appearance and costume details to the Monkey King character image in *Havoc in Heaven* for which Meiying Film Studio claims protection. Fourth, Tiansing Company argued that the Monkey King is a character from the historical novel *Journey to the West* and that its design inspiration came from the public domain. However, apart from providing the book *Journey to the West: A Pictorial Record* by Zhang Guangyu, it provided no other evidence to prove that the Monkey King character image existed historically, nor did it provide any original drafts or manuscripts. Accordingly, the court held that the Monkey King character images used by the above defendants were copied from the Monkey King character image for which Zhang Guangyu and Meiying Film Studio hold copyright. As to the specific form of infringement, the court held that the rights enjoyed by a copyright owner are exclusive rights to control specific acts. In this case, the acts of trademark registration, copyright registration, and patent application by the defendants, as alleged by Meiying Film Studio, are not acts exclusively controlled by the copyright owner. Meiying Film Studio's allegation that the defendants infringed its copyright through the above acts lacks a legal basis. However, the copyright owner has the exclusive right to control acts of information network dissemination, reproduction, and distribution. The defendants' use of the Monkey King character image on their websites constitutes an infringement of the right of information network dissemination. The use of the Monkey King character image in the manufacture and sale of children's shoes and their packaging constitutes an infringement of the rights of reproduction and distribution. As to the persons who carried out the infringing acts and those who should bear responsibility, the court held that the Monkey King character image appeared on both the website www.wukongland.com, operated by Tiansing Company, and the website www.wukongkids.com, operated by Qianzhi Company. The title bar of the former website's homepage displayed content including "Zhuhai Sky Culture Communication Co., Ltd. / Zhuhai Tiansing International Communication Agency / Tang Zeming / wukong / Tiansing / Wukong Official Website," etc. Tiansing Company stated during the trial that it could not explain this. The latter website's homepage contained the words "Wukong Apparel" and the bolded graphic and word combination trademark No. 7162768, which is similar to the graphic and word combination trademark No. 7162768 applied for by Zhuhai Sky Culture Communication Co., Ltd. Entering the homepage of the latter website, the title bar displayed "Zhuhai Wukong Apparel Co., Ltd." In the conditions for franchise and investment attraction, it stated: "Authorized by Zhuhai Sky Culture Communication Co., Ltd., Qianzhi Company is the sole legitimate user of the 'wukong series cartoon image copyright' and the wukong trademark in domestic children's shoe products." Jiulü Company's sale of Wukong children's shoes came from authorization by Wukong Company. The upper left corner of the front of the packaging box for the involved Wukong children's shoes bore the words "Wukong image authorized by Tiansing International Communication Agency." The relevant trademarks were applied for by Zhuhai Sky Culture Communication Co., Ltd. The bottom of the packaging box bore the website addresses of Qianzhi Company and Tiansing Company. The Wukong image on the plastic cartoon figurine and pictures was essentially identical to the Wukong character image designed by Tang Zebo. Given that Tiansing Company, Wukong Company, and Qianzhi Company were interconnected and cooperated with each other in disseminating the Monkey King character image online and authorizing the production and sale of Wukong children's shoes, the court held that Tiansing Company, Wukong Company, and Qianzhi Company jointly infringed the right of information network dissemination, the right of reproduction, and the right of distribution of the Monkey King character image enjoyed by Zhang Guangyu and Meiying Film Studio. Jiulü Company, as the seller of the Wukong children's shoes, sold the shoes bearing the Monkey King character image, which constitutes an infringement of the right of distribution. Yangpai Company, as the lessor of the shop premises, did not carry out any act controlled by the exclusive rights of the copyright owner. Therefore, Meiying Film Studio's claim that Yangpai Company infringed its copyright cannot be established.

3. Issues Regarding the Method of Bearing Tort Liability

According to Article 48 of the *Copyright Law*, anyone who, without the permission of the copyright owner, reproduces, distributes, or communicates to the public their work through an information network shall bear civil liability such as cessation of infringement, elimination of adverse effects, apology, and compensation for losses. The plaintiff Meiying Film Studio's request that the defendants Tiansing Company, Wukong Company, Qianzhi Company, and Jiulü Company cease their infringing acts has factual and legal basis and should be supported. Furthermore, according to Article 53 of the *Copyright Law*, a distributor of reproductions who cannot prove the lawful source of the reproductions they distribute shall bear legal liability. Given that Jiulü Company has submitted to the court evidence proving the lawful source of the Wukong children's shoes, it shall not bear liability for damages according to law. Regarding the amount of damages, Meiying Film Studio claimed compensation based on the illegal gains of the three defendants, with the specific calculation method being: the retail price of each pair of children's shoes is calculated at RMB 128, and the retail price is three times the ex-factory price, so the profit per pair of children's shoes is approximately RMB 85.4; the three defendants have at least six general agents nationwide, with an average of 50,000 pairs of children's shoes sold per year per agent, and an average brand agency fee of RMB 25,000 per year per agent; thus, the three defendants' operating profit amounts to RMB 25.75 million. Adopting a conservative standard of 20%, they requested the court to order the defendants to compensate for losses of RMB 5.15 million. The court held that this case is a copyright infringement dispute, and Meiying Film Studio cannot directly treat the sales profit of the involved children's shoes as the profit obtained from reproducing and distributing the artistic work. Therefore, this claim by Meiying Film Studio lacks factual basis and is not credible. Given that Meiying Film Studio did not provide evidence to prove its actual losses or the illegal gains obtained by the defendants, the court made a discretionary determination based on a comprehensive consideration of factors such as the type of work, the work's popularity, market value, the infringer's subjective fault, the method of infringement, duration, scope, and consequences of the damage. Further, given that Meiying Film Studio claimed the defendants should compensate for reasonable expenses of RMB 6,774.62 for investigation, evidence collection, and notarization, but only submitted invoices for notarization fees and the purchase of children's shoes, the court supported the reasonable expenses of RMB 5,328 that were evidenced. Additionally, since the civil liability of making an apology generally applies only to remedies sought by natural persons when their personal rights are infringed, the court did not support Meiying Film Studio's request for an apology from each defendant.

Accordingly, the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 3, Item (4); Article 10, Paragraph 1, Items (5), (6), and (12); Article 11, Paragraphs 1, 2, and 4; Article 48, Paragraph 1, Item (1); Article 49; and Article 53 of the *Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China*; and Articles 7; 25, Paragraphs 1 and 2; and 26 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Copyright*, rendered the following judgment on March 23, 2012:

1. Defendants Zhuhai Tiansing Cultural Communication Co., Ltd., Zhuhai Wukong Apparel Co., Ltd., Zhuhai Qianzhi Footwear Co., Ltd., and Shanghai Jiulü Trade Development Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease infringing on the plaintiff Shanghai Animation Film Studio's property rights in the copyright of the Monkey King character image artistic work in the animated film *Havoc in Heaven* as of the effective date of this judgment;

2. Defendants Zhuhai Tiansing Cultural Communication Co., Ltd., Zhuhai Wukong Apparel Co., Ltd., and Zhuhai Qianzhi Footwear Co., Ltd. shall, within ten days of the effective date of this judgment, jointly and severally compensate the plaintiff Shanghai Animation Film Studio for economic losses and reasonable expenses totaling RMB 500,000;

3. The remaining claims of the plaintiff Shanghai Animation Film Studio are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee for this case is RMB 47,850, of which the plaintiff Shanghai Animation Film Studio shall bear RMB 21,606, and the defendants Zhuhai Tiansing Cultural Communication Co., Ltd., Zhuhai Wukong Apparel Co., Ltd., and Zhuhai Qianzhi Footwear Co., Ltd. shall jointly bear RMB 26,244.

After the first-instance judgment, Tiansing Company, dissatisfied, appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court. The grounds for appeal were: Tiansing Company lawfully owns patents, trademarks, and copyright for the Wukong cartoon image and did not infringe the appellee Meiying Film Studio's rights of information network dissemination, reproduction, and distribution. Furthermore, even if infringement existed, the amount of damages awarded in the original judgment was excessively high. Therefore, the original judgment had unclear findings and erroneous application of law. They requested the reversal of the original judgment and a new judgment in accordance with law, with all litigation costs of this case borne by the appellee.

The appellee Meiying Film Studio argued in its defense that it is the copyright owner of the film *Havoc in Heaven* and the Monkey King image therein. The appellant Tiansing Company's so-called copyright, trademark, and patent were only at the acceptance stage or promotional stage, not actually registered, and some of those animated images are irrelevant to this case. Tiansing Company's actions infringed Meiying Film Studio's lawful rights and interests. Its appeal claims lack factual and legal basis and should be dismissed.

The first-instance defendant Yangpai Company and the first-instance defendant Jiulü Company argued in their defense that they accepted the result of the original judgment and expressed no opinion on the appellant Tiansing Company's claims or the appellee Meiying Film Studio's defense.

The first-instance defendants Wukong Company and Qianzhi Company did not submit defense opinions to the court.

During the second instance, none of the parties submitted new evidence.

The Shanghai High People's Court, upon trial in the second instance, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

It was additionally found that the design patent titled "Toy," Patent No. ZL03325153.3, was filed on June 3, 2003, published and granted on May 5, 2004, with Tang Zebo as the patentee.

Among the trademark registration certificates, trademark files, and trademark registration application acceptance notices provided by the appellant Tiansing Company during the first instance, only the "WuKong" graphic and word combination trademark with Application No. 5585913 and the graphic and word combination trademark with Application No. 7162768 relate to the footwear goods of International Class 25 involved in this case. Trademark No. 5585913 was filed on September 4, 2006, and Trademark No. 7162768 was filed on January 13, 2009.

During the second-instance trial, the appellant Tiansing Company stated it had no objection to the reasonable expenses determined in the first-instance judgment.

The Shanghai High People's Court held in the second instance that the appellee Meiying Film Studio and Zhang Guangyu jointly own the copyright property rights in the Monkey King character image artistic work in the animated film *Havoc in Heaven*. In this case, the allegedly infringing Monkey King character image is substantially similar in main features to the Monkey King character image artistic work in *Havoc in Heaven*. Since none of the users could prove a lawful basis for using the allegedly infringing image, their unauthorized use of the Meiying Film Studio's involved work on the internet, on children's shoe products, and on their packaging constitutes infringement of the work's copyright property rights, and they shall each bear their corresponding civil liability for infringement.

In this case, the appellant Tiansing Company and the first-instance defendant Qianzhi Company used the allegedly infringing Monkey King character image on their websites, constituting infringement of the appellee Meiying Film Studio's right of information network dissemination in the involved work. The first-instance defendant Jiulü Company, authorized by Wukong Company, sold children's shoes bearing the said Monkey King character image, also infringing Meiying Film Studio's rights of reproduction and distribution in the involved work. Given that the title bar of Tiansing Company's website homepage displayed content including "Zhuhai Sky Culture Communication Co., Ltd. / Zhuhai Tiansing International Communication Agency / Tang Zeming / wukong / Tiansing / Wukong Official Website," etc.; and that Qianzhi Company set up a Wukong Company section on its website, stating it was authorized by Sky Culture Company to use the "wukong series cartoon images" and related trademarks; and that the packaging box of the infringing children's shoes sold by Jiulü Company also bore the words "Wukong image authorized by Tiansing International Communication Agency," with the bottom of the packaging box further indicating the website information of Qianzhi Company and Tiansing Company; therefore, the original judgment's finding that Tiansing Company, Qianzhi Company, and Wukong Company had a meeting of minds in the above infringing acts and should bear joint civil liability for infringement has factual and legal basis. Jiulü Company, as the seller of the infringing product, may not bear liability for damages according to law if it can provide the lawful source of the product, but it must still bear civil liability for ceasing the infringement of Meiying Film Studio's right of distribution in the involved work. Yangpai Company, as the lessor of the shop premises, did not carry out any act infringing Meiying Film Studio's copyright property rights in the involved work in this case, and therefore should not bear civil liability for infringement.

The appellant Tiansing Company argued that it lawfully owns patents, trademarks, and copyright for the Wukong cartoon image and did not infringe the appellee Meiying Film Studio's rights of information network dissemination, reproduction, and distribution. The court held that, firstly, according to the evidence provided by Tiansing Company in this case, the dates of its design patent right, trademark right, and artistic work copyright registration are all far later than the time when Meiying Film Studio completed the involved work. According to the basic principle of "protecting prior rights" for resolving intellectual property rights conflicts, Tiansing Company cannot use rights obtained later to oppose the rights obtained earlier by Meiying Film Studio. Secondly, even if the allegedly infringing Monkey King character image is compared with the design patent, artistic work provided by Tiansing Company, and Meiying Film Studio's involved work, the similarity between the allegedly infringing Monkey King character image and Meiying Film Studio's involved work is far greater than the similarity between that image and Tiansing Company's design patent and artistic work. For example, according to the trademark application files provided by Tiansing Company, the graphic and word combination trademark with Application No. 5585913 "WuKong" contains the head image of the Monkey King image from Tiansing Company's design patent, while the graphic and word combination trademark with Application No. 7162768 contains only a simplified silhouette of the Monkey King head. The graphics contained in the above trademarks are not similar to the allegedly infringing Monkey King character image. Therefore, the above application files also cannot support Tiansing Company's defense that it had a lawful basis for using the allegedly infringing image. In summary, Tiansing Company's above reasons lack factual and legal basis and are not supported.

The appellant Tiansing Company further argued that the amount of damages awarded in the original judgment was excessively high. In this regard, the court held that, according to the provisions of the *Copyright Law* and relevant judicial interpretations, if the actual losses of the copyright owner or the illegal gains of the infringer cannot be determined, the people's court shall, based on the circumstances of the infringement, decide on compensation of up to RMB 500,000. The amount of compensation shall also include the reasonable expenses incurred by the right holder to stop the infringement. In this case, the appellee Meiying Film Studio's involved Monkey King character image artistic work is highly renowned and has enormous market value. In the absence of evidence proving the actual losses suffered by Meiying Film Studio due to the infringement or the actual profits gained by the infringer, the first-instance court's discretionary determination of the total amount of damages and reasonable expenses at RMB 500,000, considering factors such as the type, popularity, and market value of the work in this case, the nature, circumstances, and consequences of the infringing acts, and the reasonable expenses incurred by the right holder to stop the infringement, was not inappropriate. Therefore, the appellant's above reason is not supported.

In conclusion, the appellant Tiansing Company's appeal requests and reasons lack factual and legal basis and should be dismissed. Accordingly, the Shanghai High People's Court, pursuant to Article 84, Article 130, Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1), and Article 157 of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, rendered the following judgment on December 8, 2012:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

The case acceptance fee for the second instance is RMB 8,800, to be borne by the appellant Zhuhai Tiansing Cultural Communication Co., Ltd.
